newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - German union proposes 32-hour week.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German union proposes 32-hour week.

text.p: Germany's largest trade union, IG Metall, seized the initiative at a high-profile jobs conference on Wednesday by proposing a 32-hour working week to help slash the country's record unemployment.

Klaus Zwickel, chairman of the union which also ranks as the western world's largest, for the first time also made clear that his union would be ready to accept a partial reduction in wages linked to the shorter working hours.

Zwickel last year grabbed headlines by initiating the "Alliance for Jobs" pact with government and employers, which ultimately failed. He said the first step to such a work reduction would be the 35-hour week currently being implemented in the metal and engineering sectors it represents.

"A 35-hour week, together with a reduction in overtime and increased part-time work, must be introduced in all industry sectors," Zwickel told the 500-plus trade unionists, employers and politicians that attended the conference.
He added that a 35-hour week would be written into the contracts of all the roughly four million workers in the west German metal and engineering sectors by the end of next year.

"(We will then) concentrate on the implementation of a general 32-hour week and four-day weeks for individual workers", he said, saying such a measure would help tackle to country's current 4.5 million jobless total.

The move to shorter working hours was pushed through by IG Metall amid great triumph in the early 1990's. Then, it negotiated that wages should remain unchanged despite the smaller number of hours worked by the individual employee.

This time, however, Zwickel said that the move to 32-hours would be "scarcely achievable" without some reduction in wages. "But a completely proportional cut in wages is also hardly acceptable," he added.
IG Metall would be willing to discuss various ways in which wages could be reduced according to individual income groups or according to accompanying job creation measures, Zwickel said.

He added that the Federal Labour Office, through which unemployment benefits are paid, could make a financial contribution to such schemes as a result of the drop in joblessness that could be expected to follow.

The IG Metall plan was the one concrete proposal to emerge from a two-day jobs conference that was long on polemic but short on substance, but was swiftly shot down by Gesamtmetall, the employers federation of the metal and engineering industry.
"A general 32-hour workweek anchored in pay contracts is rejected in the strongest terms, completely independently of the level of pay compensation offered," it said in a statement.
"Nowhere in the world is a cut in working time used as a means in the battle against unemployment," Gesamtmetall said.

Despite Gesamtmetall's opposition, Zwickel has shown in the past a knack in pushing through his union's agenda and, with the "Alliance for Jobs", nearly got Bonn and employers to agree to an ambitious job creation plan early last year.

But that plan ended in accusations of betrayal as trade unions balked at the welfare and social benefit cuts that were finally included in Bonn's austerity package in the run-up to European monetary union.

Any hopes that the government might support any new debate on working hours were quashed at the jobs conference when Wolfgang Schaeuble, parliamentary leader of Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats, said politicians had no role there.
"On the matter of working hours, union and employer wage negotiators are better placed to solve the conflict than politicians," Schaeuble said.

He did however hold out some hope that in forthcoming talks over the major tax reform planned that a way could be found of reducing the high supplementary costs associated with employing people in Germany.
Asked if such a refinancing of so-called non-wage labour costs could be done in other ways such as a value-added tax, he said: "To a certain extent yes. That is something we can talk about."

Oskar Lafontaine, head of the opposition Social Democrats, said the fact that most European governments were currently seeking to reduce corporate taxes could lead to them seeking revenues elsewhere, for example in raising wage taxes and contributions.

He warned that this would make labour more expensive and lead to greater unemployment and repeated calls that as a result a European-wide commitment to employment creation was needed with the currency union treaty.
